title: Ways a Sickness Can Spread
statement:
n people stand in a row, at positions 0 to n − 1. The people at the positions in sick (sorted, distinct) are already ill; everyone else is healthy.

Every second, exactly one healthy person who stands right next to an ill person becomes ill. This repeats until everyone is ill. The order in which the initially healthy people fall ill is an infection sequence.

Return how many different infection sequences are possible, modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: The gap 1, 2, 3 is eaten from its left or right end. Two free choices, then the last person is forced: 2 × 2 = 4.
Person 0 can only be reached from 1, and 3 only after 2. The valid orders are 0 2 3, 2 0 3 and 2 3 0.
Gaps {1} and {3, 4}. Interleave 1 item with 2 items in 3 ways; the 2-person gap can go 3 then 4 or 4 then 3: 3 × 2 = 6.

constraints: sick is sorted increasingly, values in [0, n − 1], all distinct
hints: The sick people cut the row into separate gaps. Inside one gap, which people can be infected next?
An end gap (before the first or after the last sick person) can only be eaten from one side: one order. An inner gap of length g is eaten from either end, giving 2^(g−1) orders.

Now interleave the gaps: with m healthy people in total and gaps g₁, g₂, …, the number of ways to merge the sequences is m! / (g₁! g₂! …). Multiply by the inner-gap factors, using modular inverses for the division.

explain.intuition:
Split the problem into two independent parts. First, inside each gap: an end gap touches ill people on one side only, so it is infected from that side in a single fixed order. An inner gap of length g has an ill person at both ends, so each step takes its leftmost or rightmost healthy person; that is a free choice for the first g − 1 steps and forced for the last, giving 2^(g−1) orders.

Second, between gaps: gaps never affect each other, so a full sequence is any interleaving of the per-gap sequences. Interleaving lists of lengths g₁, g₂, … with m items in total gives the multinomial m! / (g₁! g₂! …). Multiply both parts. Under a prime modulus, division becomes multiplication by an inverse factorial, computed with Fermat's little theorem.
steps: Collect the gaps: sick[0] on the left, n − 1 − sick[last] on the right, and sick[i] − sick[i−1] − 1 between neighbours.
Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to n modulo 1 000 000 007.
Start with m! where m = n − sick.length, and multiply by the inverse factorial of every gap length.
For each inner gap with g > 0, multiply by 2^(g−1).
pitfalls: Giving the end gaps a factor of 2^(g−1) too. They spread from one side only.
Using 2^g instead of 2^(g−1) for inner gaps. The last person in a gap is the same whichever side you pick.
Dividing with / under the modulus. You need modular inverses, and in JavaScript products up to 10¹⁸ need BigInt.

solutions.title: Count over sets of ill people
solutions.idea: Memoised search over the bitmask of who is ill: the count from a state is the sum over each person who can fall ill next.

solutions.title: Multinomial times inner-gap choices
solutions.idea: m! / Π gᵢ! ways to interleave the gaps, times 2^(g−1) for each non-empty inner gap.

solutions.title: Merge gaps one at a time with binomials
solutions.idea: Insert the gaps one by one: a gap of g people can be merged into the p people placed so far in C(p + g, g) ways.

followups: People stand in a circle instead of a row. Which gaps change their factor?
